items.prompt: What is calibration?
choices: A session where managers compare drafts against one rubric
A private one-on-one talk between a manager and a single report
A yearly company survey sent out to every employee
items.explanation: Calibration is a comparison across managers, before ratings are final.

items.prompt: When does calibration happen relative to final ratings?
choices: After they are announced to everyone
Before they are finalized
Only when a report objects to theirs
items.explanation: Its purpose is to adjust drafts, so it must come first.

items.prompt: What is a calibration packet?
choices: A summary of how likeable the person is to the team
The manager's overall gut feeling about the person
Written evidence with examples, dates and outcomes
items.explanation: A packet replaces impressions with specifics.

items.prompt: Why can one manager not fix their own distortion alone?
choices: Biases do not feel like bias from inside
Managers refuse to read through their own notes
Ratings are always set by the company, not by managers
items.explanation: The distortion is invisible to the person who has it.

items.prompt: What does calibration aim for?
choices: Every person receiving an identical final rating
The same quality of work earning the same rating
Managers becoming more popular with their teams
items.explanation: Consistency across teams is the goal, not uniform outcomes.

items.prompt: Which is stronger evidence in a packet?
choices: The word 'excellent' repeated three times
A feeling that things went well
A dated example with its outcome
items.explanation: Specifics can be checked; adjectives cannot.

items.prompt: Why compare drafts side by side?
choices: A gap between managers makes a hidden distortion visible
It lets the loudest manager decide the outcome quickly
It makes every meeting shorter for the people attending
items.explanation: Inconsistency between drafts is the signal.

items.prompt: Who benefits when calibration works?
choices: Only people with the most visible launches
People whose work was easy to overlook
Only managers who write the longest reviews
items.explanation: It protects quiet or older contributions from being lost.

items.prompt: Two managers rate comparable work a 2 and a 4 because one rates strictly and one generously. Neither is dishonest. What does calibration offer?
choices: A rule that every manager must give the same average rating across their teams
A shared rubric and side-by-side drafts that expose the gap
A request that the stricter manager simply start rating more generously from now on
A vote where the majority rating wins without any check of the evidence
items.explanation: The gap between managers is the signal; the rubric and evidence give a basis to resolve it rather than averaging or voting.
items.reference:
What calibration compares
each manager: draft rating + evidence packet
the group: all drafts side by side, one rubric
result: same work earns the same rating on any team
Why: a single manager cannot see their own distortion, but a room comparing drafts can.
items.learnMore:
Calibration and the packet

Calibration is a comparison step before ratings are final. The packet (dated examples and outcomes) is what makes the comparison about facts rather than impressions.

Common mistake

Treating calibration as a meeting where managers vouch for their people with enthusiasm instead of with evidence.
items.reflection: Think of a time two people were judged by different standards, at work or at school. Who could have noticed the gap, and how?

items.prompt: A manager arrives with a rating of 4 and the note 'one of the best people I have managed.' What is missing for calibration?
choices: Dated examples and outcomes others can check against the rubric
A longer description of the person's character and working style
Confirmation that the manager sincerely believes in the rating
A comparison with how the manager was rated in earlier years
items.explanation: Sincerity is assumed; calibration needs checkable specifics.

items.prompt: Why is calibration run before ratings are final rather than after a report complains?
choices: Reports are not allowed to question a rating once it is finished
Managers need extra time to prepare their own defense of it
Complaints nearly always come from people with weak results
Fixing a draft is cheap, while reversing a delivered rating costs trust
items.explanation: Once a rating is delivered, changing it is slow and damages credibility.

choices: Every rating ends up identical to the first draft that was submitted
The most senior manager overrules the others after a quick glance
A draft is revised after the group asks what evidence supports it
The meeting ends early because nobody asked a single question
items.explanation: Calibration works when evidence questions change or confirm a rating on the facts.

items.prompt: A review cites only last month's launch. Which bias is this?
choices: Halo effect
Recency bias
Central tendency
items.explanation: Recent events crowd out older work.

items.prompt: One great result raises marks on unrelated skills. Which bias is this?
choices: Recency bias
Leniency
Halo effect
items.explanation: A single strong trait spills onto everything.

items.prompt: A manager rates every report a 3 to avoid hard talks. Which bias?
choices: Central tendency
Halo effect
Recency bias
items.explanation: Clustering in the middle avoids differentiation.

items.prompt: A manager habitually rates everyone high. Which bias?
choices: Recency bias
Leniency
Halo effect
items.explanation: It is a personal habit, independent of the actual spread.

items.prompt: Which bias is about the manager's habit, not the person rated?
choices: Recency bias alone
The halo effect alone
Leniency or central tendency
items.explanation: The other two depend on events or traits of the person.

items.prompt: In the unit's model, which work is more likely recalled in December?
choices: The November launch
The February fix
They are equally likely
items.explanation: Recall fades with time, so recent work is cited more often.

items.prompt: Does a recency-biased review have to contain false statements?
choices: Yes, because bias always involves lying outright
No, it can be true and still incomplete
Yes, otherwise the review would simply be fair
items.explanation: The distortion is in what is left out.

items.prompt: Rating someone high on mentoring without ever seeing them mentor is?
choices: Recency bias
Central tendency
Halo effect
items.explanation: The rating rests on a trait observed elsewhere.

items.prompt: Wren's review praises mentoring, though the manager has only seen the launch. Which bias is this, and what exposes it?
choices: Recency bias: a rating with no evidence from earlier quarters of the year
Leniency: one manager rates above every other manager in the room
Halo effect: a rating on an area nobody observed
Central tendency: every dimension receives the same middle score
items.explanation: The launch inflates an area never observed. The tell is a rating without evidence for that specific dimension.
items.reference:
Three distortions, three signatures
recency: detailed recent examples, nothing older
halo: strong marks in areas never observed
leniency / central tendency: one manager clusters apart from the rest
Why: each bias leaves a different trace, so telling them apart tells you what to ask.
items.learnMore:
Recency, halo, leniency

Recency is about when the work happened, halo is about one strong trait spilling over onto others, and leniency or central tendency is about the manager's habit rather than the person.

Common mistake

Calling any inflated review 'halo effect' without checking whether the manager actually observed the other areas.
items.reflection: Think of a judgment you made about someone based on one vivid moment. What older or less visible moments did you leave out?

items.prompt: Dan gives all eight reports a 3, while other managers use the full scale for similar spreads of work. Which pattern is this, and what shows it?
choices: Recency bias: his packets cite only the latest work from the year
Central tendency: his ratings cluster tighter than the others'
Halo effect: one strong result lifted ratings across the whole team
Leniency: his average sits above every other manager's average
items.explanation: Clustering at the middle is a manager-level habit, visible only by comparing his spread with others.
items.reference:

halo: strong marks in areas never observed
leniency / central tendency: one manager clusters apart from the rest

items.prompt: A packet has rich detail from October and November and none from the first nine months. What should the room ask?
choices: What specific examples exist from the earlier months of the year?
Whether the manager is being lenient toward this particular team
Whether the person benefits from a strong halo across several areas
Whether the rating should drop for lack of any recent growth
items.explanation: The shape of the evidence points at recency; the fix is asking for the older material.

items.prompt: Why tell the three biases apart rather than just asking managers to be fair?
choices: Naming a bias once makes the manager immune to it in all later review cycles
Only one of the three affects ratings in practice at all
Each bias needs its own separate rating scale in the rubric
Each leaves a different trace and calls for a different question
items.explanation: Recency asks for older evidence, halo for observed evidence, leniency for cross-manager comparison.

items.prompt: When are calibration drafts written?
choices: Live, while the whole group watches
Right after the ratings are finalized
Independently, before the session
items.explanation: Private drafts prevent anchoring.

items.prompt: What is the first question about a thin packet?
choices: What specific dated example supports it?
Who is arguing for it most loudly in the room?
Is it really a 3, or is it a 4?
items.explanation: Evidence is checkable; the number is not yet.

items.prompt: Why not start by debating the number?
choices: Numbers cannot be discussed in meetings
It becomes a contest of gut impressions
It would make the session far too long
items.explanation: Without evidence, the more persuasive person tends to win.

items.prompt: What does an independent draft prevent?
choices: Managers from writing down any evidence
Any disagreement between the managers
Everyone anchoring on the first speaker
items.explanation: Anchoring hides real differences.

items.prompt: Which packets does the room discuss first?
choices: Outliers and thin packets
Only the very highest ratings
Whichever manager wrote the most
items.explanation: Outliers are where a distortion is most likely.

items.prompt: If the evidence supports a rating, what happens?
choices: It is lowered anyway
The rating stands
It waits for the next meeting
items.explanation: Calibration confirms ratings as well as revising them.

items.prompt: If the evidence does not support a rating, what happens?
choices: The manager is replaced right away
Nothing happens and the draft is just kept
The manager revises it or gathers more
items.explanation: A gap is a reason to look again.

items.prompt: Why does evidence-first catch recency bias?
choices: A packet with nothing from earlier months looks thin
It forces managers to recall every single date correctly
It removes the rubric from the discussion completely
items.explanation: Missing older material becomes visible.

items.prompt: A room skips independent drafts and the most senior manager speaks first, giving a 4. What is the likely effect on the others?
choices: Their ratings spread further away from the first speaker's number
They write much longer evidence packets to make up for it
They set the rubric aside and just rely on that first rating
Their ratings drift toward that 4 and real disagreement stays hidden
items.explanation: Anchoring pulls later judgments toward the first number and masks differences.
items.reference:
Order of the session
1. independent draft + evidence
2. drafts shared before the meeting
3. outliers and thin packets first
4. 'what dated example?' before 'what number?'
Why: private commitment prevents anchoring and evidence turns a negotiation into a fact-check.
items.learnMore:
Independent drafts, evidence first

Writing drafts alone keeps the room from anchoring on the first speaker. Asking for evidence before the number gives everyone a shared, checkable question.

Common mistake

Opening with 'is this a 3 or a 4,' which invites persuasion contests instead of fact checks.
items.reflection: Think of a group decision where the first person to speak shaped the outcome. How could you have asked for independent input first?

items.prompt: Two managers disagree on a 3 versus a 4. Which opening question produces the most progress?
choices: Which of the two of you has managed this person for longer?
Can we split the difference at 3.5 and move on to the next one?
Which dated example separates a 4 from a 3 here?
Which rating would the stricter of you normally prefer to use?
items.explanation: A shared, checkable question replaces a negotiation.

Ask for dated evidence from those two quarters before accepting the rating
Lower the rating by one point as a precaution against the gap
Move it to the end of the agenda so it gets less attention

Asking managers to write longer summary paragraphs about each person
Having managers re-rate their reports again from memory alone
Holding the meeting later in the year than the group usually does

items.prompt: What does a single 'did great work' bar mostly measure?
choices: Raw output and visible impact
Quality of teamwork alone, everywhere
Hours spent in meetings
items.explanation: It rewards whoever produces more.

items.prompt: Who wins on raw output by default?
choices: The person with the narrower scope
The person with the wider scope
Nobody, it is always a tie
items.explanation: Wider scope produces more by being wider.

items.prompt: What does a per-scope rubric do?
choices: Gives everyone the very same set of tasks
Removes the need for any evidence at all
Names what meeting expectations means per band
items.explanation: Each person is judged against their own bar.

items.prompt: A narrow-scope engineer delivers scoped work reliably. Against their own band, this is?
choices: Meeting expectations
Always below expectations
Irrelevant to the final rating
items.explanation: Reliable scoped delivery is the bar for that band.

items.prompt: What might a wider-scope band measure?
choices: Typing speed on assigned tasks
Spotting problems nobody assigned
Length of time spent at the company
items.explanation: Self-directed problem finding is the wider-scope signal.

items.prompt: Should the rubric come from the organization's own ladder?
choices: No, any table found online works just as well
No, a rubric should never be used
Yes, a generic table is only an illustration
items.explanation: The ladder defines the real expectations.

items.prompt: Without a rubric per scope, comparison becomes?
choices: Who did more
Who met their own bar
Who is the most senior
items.explanation: Output volume becomes the hidden yardstick.

items.prompt: Who can be unfairly overlooked with one shared bar?
choices: Only the most visible launches of the year
Excellent work at a narrower scope
Nobody at all, since it is neutral
items.explanation: Their well-scoped work looks small beside wider output.

items.prompt: A room rates an engineer on narrow assigned tasks and another who finds unassigned problems, using one bar: 'impact delivered.' What distortion appears?
choices: The wider scope wins and the narrower engineer looks thin
The narrower scope wins because assigned tasks are easier to finish
Both get the same rating regardless of the work that was done
The more recent worker wins no matter how large their scope was
items.explanation: Output grows with scope, so one output-based bar systematically favors the wider scope.
items.reference:
One bar vs. a bar per scope
one bar: 'did great work' measures raw output
wider scope produces more output by default
per-scope rubric: judge each against their own band
Why: a shared bar quietly turns the comparison into who did more.
items.learnMore:
Rubrics by scope

A rubric states what meeting expectations measures at each scope band, such as reliable delivery of assigned tasks versus finding unassigned problems.

Common mistake

Copying a generic table of scope bands instead of using the organization's own career ladder.
items.reflection: Think of two people in very different roles being compared by one yardstick. What did that yardstick really measure?

items.prompt: Why can a single bar also be unfair to the wider-scope engineer?
choices: They are held to an impossible standard of raw output every year
Their work is much harder to describe in a written packet
More people are available to speak up for them in the room
They can coast on scale instead of doing what their band expects
items.explanation: A shared bar rewards volume instead of the specific things a wider scope should add, like finding unassigned problems.

items.prompt: Is Dan's draft for Sam dishonest?
choices: Yes, it contains outright falsehoods
No, it is true but thin
Yes, simply because it is short
items.explanation: Nothing in it is false; it just lacks specifics.

items.prompt: What does Dan's draft lack?
choices: A positive tone overall
The word 'reliable' in it
A specific, dated example
items.explanation: No example, no date, no outcome.

items.prompt: What does the room ask Dan first?
choices: What dated evidence supports the 3?
Why he seems to dislike Sam so much
Whether Sam is hoping for a raise
items.explanation: Evidence is the starting question.

items.prompt: What did Sam do in February?
choices: Launched the checkout redesign
Caught a flaw that would have corrupted records
Left the team for a few weeks
items.explanation: A quiet prevention nobody outside the team saw.

items.prompt: Why did almost nobody hear about Sam's fix?
choices: Sam deliberately kept it a secret
The fix was never actually completed
Nothing broke, so nothing was visible
items.explanation: Prevented problems leave no visible event.

items.prompt: Does Wren's packet get checked too?
choices: Yes, every packet gets the same fact-check
No, strong packets are exempt from it
No, only Dan's packet is ever checked
items.explanation: Checking only surprising packets lets bias through elsewhere.

items.prompt: What changed Sam's rating from 3 to 4?
choices: Dan simply arguing more loudly than before
Documented evidence matched against the rubric
Wren's rating going down to balance it
items.explanation: The rating changed because the evidence did.

items.prompt: Which bias shaped Dan's draft?
choices: Halo effect
Central tendency
Recency bias
items.explanation: Sam's work was old and quiet, so it faded.

items.prompt: Dan insists, sincerely, that 'Sam has been solid all year.' How should the room treat that?
choices: Accept it, because Dan knows Sam better than anyone in the room
Ask for dated examples, since sincerity alone is not evidence
Treat it as a sign that Dan is being dishonest about Sam
Raise the rating because Dan sounds so confident when he says it
items.explanation: Calibration checks the backing of a claim rather than the manager's conviction.
items.reference:
Dan's packet vs. what the room asks
draft: 'solid, reliable, nothing stands out'
missing: example, date, outcome
room asks: what dated evidence is behind the 3?
answer: February migration fix, documented
Why: a thin packet is true but faint, and only a request for specifics shows it.
items.learnMore:
True but thin

A draft can be completely honest and still unfair if its evidence has faded to a general impression. Calibration checks backing, not sincerity.

Common mistake

Assuming that a confident, sincere manager must have complete evidence.
